title: Why Big Tech’s AI Spending is $3 Trillion Higher than it Seems: Alphabet (GOOGL) & Meta Platforms (META)

content_html:
Fatima Gulzar

Fri, August 28, 2026 at 11:35 AM EDT 4 min read

On August 16, 2026, the Wall Street Journal reported that nine major technology companies, including Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META), carry roughly $3 trillion in AI-related commitments that do not appear on their balance sheets. That figure is about five times the roughly $600 billion in capital expenditures the companies reported over the past year and about triple their combined on-balance-sheet lease and debt liabilities, the Journal found. The companies show $248 billion in leases on their balance sheets but carry roughly $900 billion to $1.2 trillion more off of them and disclose $356 billion in on-balance-sheet debt, separate from roughly $1.9 trillion in additional purchase commitments the Journal identified.

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) alone has accumulated an estimated $811 billion in purchase commitments, up sharply from $322 billion three months earlier, according to the Journal's data.

Bull Case

Off-balance-sheet financing is legitimate. It is a widely used accounting tool, not evidence of trouble on its own. Structuring long-term data center leases and chip purchase agreements this way is standard practice under current accounting rules. It lets companies like Alphabet and Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) commit to AI infrastructure without immediately inflating reported debt, preserving financial flexibility and credit ratings while capacity gets built.

The scale of these commitments shows contracted demand rather than speculative spending. Optimists see soaring demand for AI tools, which has already produced hardware shortages, as evidence that revenue to cover these obligations will materialize over time. Companies do not typically sign multi-year, multi-billion-dollar purchase and lease commitments without confidence in the underlying demand driving them.

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) specifically has a track record that supports this kind of aggressive capital commitment. Alphabet's own reported return on prior technology investment has historically been strong. As one of the most cash-generative companies in the index, it has the operating cash flow to support large purchase commitments without the same balance-sheet strain a smaller or less profitable company would face.

Bear Case

The obligations are growing faster than the reported spending investors already track. The Journal found off-balance-sheet AI commitments are expanding faster than traditional capex. It means the headline capital-spending figures companies report each quarter increasingly understate the real financial exposure shareholders are underwriting.
